## The whole book, in five steps

\begin{block}{ALGORITHM 1.1 --- Bayes}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Write down a \textbf{likelihood}.
\item Write down a \textbf{prior}.
\item Put the data in.
\item Turn the crank --- Bayes' theorem.
\item \textbf{Criticize your model.}
\end{enumerate}
\end{block}

\vspace{0.5em}

Steps 1--4 are Chapter 1. Step 5 is Chapter 2.

Everything after that --- regression, MCMC, panels, time series --- is these same five steps on
harder models.

## Two sessions

**Session 1 --- the machine**

Appendix 1 $\cdot$ Bayes' theorem $\cdot$ the algorithm $\cdot$ the likelihood $\cdot$
exchangeability $\cdot$ prior $\cdot$ posterior

\vspace{0.6em}

**Session 2 --- what you do with it**

Monte Carlo and ABC $\cdot$ prediction $\cdot$ decisions and Wald $\cdot$ value at risk

\vspace{0.6em}

Detail, quotes and derivations live in the extended deck.

# I. What are we even doing?

## An econometric analysis

**The confrontation of an economic model with evidence.**

\vspace{0.6em}

It asks two questions:

1. **Is the model consistent with the evidence?** $\to$ Chapter 2
2. **If so, which structures are probable?** $\to$ Chapter 1

\vspace{0.6em}

In practice we ask them backwards: assume it fits, then find the probable structures.

## Econometrics is not statistics

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
**Statistics**

Reduce a pile of numbers to something a mind can hold.

Data first.
:::
::: {.column width="47%"}
**Econometrics**

Explain the behavior of **agents** in markets.

Data second.
:::
::::

\vspace{0.7em}

That is why our models have equilibrium, optimization, and agents who know things we don't ---
and why our parameters mean something.

\vspace{0.5em}

\socratic{An elasticity of substitution exists only inside a theory.
\textbf{In what sense can such a thing be \emph{true}?}}

# II. Appendix 1 --- the conversion manual

## The frequentist picture

Everyone here was trained this way. Appendix 1 is not an argument --- **it is a map of what changes.**

\vspace{0.5em}

- There is a **population**. Your data are a **sample** from it.
- There is a **true** $\theta_0$.
- You pick an **estimator** --- a formula.
- You judge that formula by how it behaves **over samples you never saw**.

\vspace{0.6em}

Bias, variance, MSE, power, consistency: **every one is an average over imaginary data.**

## The Bayesian picture

- You have **beliefs** about $\theta$, and data in hand.
- Bayes' theorem tells you how the data **change** the beliefs.
- You report the resulting distribution.

\vspace{0.8em}

\key{Frequentist inference conditions on a $\theta$ you never learn.\\
Bayesian inference conditions on the data you actually have.}

## What actually changes

\begin{block}{Four of Lancaster's eight}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Bayes \textbf{demands more}: a full likelihood, not just a moment condition.
\item There is only \textbf{one estimator} --- the posterior. Model and data imply it.
\item Bias, MSE, efficiency are \textbf{irrelevant} --- including Gauss--Markov.
\item Consistency asks what happens \textbf{with more data than you have}.
\end{enumerate}
\end{block}

## The bus example

200 Bay Area commuters. You toss a coin for each: bus or car.

You end up with **97 bus, 103 car**.

\vspace{0.6em}

Now the frequentist must decide what to imagine repeating:

- samples of size 97 and 103?
- or 200 coin tosses, with the counts moving around?

\vspace{0.5em}

**The standard errors differ.** The Bayesian conditions on 97 and 103 and never notices.

## Ask the room

\socratic{
Your standard errors changed because of a coin toss that has nothing to do with commuting.

\vspace{0.4em}
Cox \& Hinkley say: condition on what you actually saw.

\vspace{0.4em}
\textbf{Once you start conditioning, how far can you go before you have become a Bayesian?}
}

## Sometimes the numbers agree

$n$ normal draws, known variance. Both camps report the same interval.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
**Frequentist**

"95% of intervals built this way would contain $\mu$."

A claim about the **procedure**.
:::
::: {.column width="47%"}
**Bayesian**

"The probability that $\mu$ is in here is 0.95."

A claim about **$\mu$**.
:::
::::

\vspace{0.6em}

Same numbers. Only one of them is the sentence you actually wanted to say.

# III. The algorithm

## Bayes' theorem

$$p(\theta \mid y) \;\propto\; p(y \mid \theta)\;p(\theta)$$

\vspace{0.5em}

**Posterior $\propto$ likelihood $\times$ prior.**

\vspace{0.8em}

Nobody disputes the theorem. The disputes are about two other things:

- what probability **means**
- what it may be **applied to**

## Probability means degree of belief

The larger $P(A)$, the more strongly you believe $A$.

\vspace{0.6em}

That is what lets an analysis end with:

> "In the light of the evidence, theory A is very unlikely and theory B is quite probable."

\vspace{0.6em}

**In traditional econometrics that sentence is illegal.** Theories are true or false, not probable.

## What may have a probability?

Frequentists: only things embedded in a repeatable sequence.

\vspace{0.6em}

Lancaster: anything you have beliefs about.

- the US was in recession in 1983
- the moon is made of green cheese
- the economy is in general equilibrium

\vspace{0.6em}

There is no sequence of worlds in some of which 1983 was a recession.

## Evidence moving a belief

Two structures. You think each is 50/50.

The data are **unlikely** under structure 1 ($0.1$), **likely** under structure 2 ($0.6$).

\vspace{0.6em}

$$\text{prior odds } 1:1 \quad\longrightarrow\quad \textbf{posterior odds } 6:1$$

\vspace{0.6em}

The evidence entered as a **ratio**, $0.6/0.1$. Nothing else about the data mattered.

## Two ways evidence fails to move you

\begin{block}{You were dogmatic}
If you gave a theory probability zero, no data can ever raise it.\\
\textbf{"If you gave no credence at all to a theory you will never learn that it is right."}
\end{block}

\begin{block}{The data can't tell them apart}
If both structures make the data equally probable, the data say nothing.
\end{block}

\vspace{0.4em}

Make the second one true for *every possible dataset* and you have **non-identification**.

## Parameters and data

\begin{block}{The only distinction that matters}
A \textbf{parameter} is unknown to you before the data \emph{and after}.\\
\textbf{Data} are unknown before and \textbf{known after}.
\end{block}

\vspace{0.6em}

That's it. So a parameter can be a constant, a whole theory, or an unknown function.

\vspace{0.5em}

And "random" vs. "fixed" stops meaning anything: **everything unknown gets a distribution.**

## The algorithm again

\begin{block}{ALGORITHM 1.1}
\textbf{1.} likelihood \quad \textbf{2.} prior \quad \textbf{3.} data \quad
\textbf{4.} Bayes' theorem \quad \textbf{5.} criticize
\end{block}

\vspace{0.6em}

Steps 1--4 are mechanical once you commit.

\vspace{0.4em}

**Step 5 is the only step where the world gets to talk back.**

\vspace{0.6em}

Which is why Chapter 2 is not an appendix to Chapter 1. It is the other half.

# IV. The likelihood --- the information transfer function

## One object, two names

$$p(y \mid \theta) \qquad\text{vs.}\qquad \ell(\theta ; y)$$

- Before the data: a **distribution over data**, given $\theta$.
- After the data: a **function of $\theta$**, with your data baked in.

\vspace{0.6em}

Note the semicolon. It is **not** a probability distribution for $\theta$.

\vspace{0.5em}

\key{This is the only door the data come through. Prior in, posterior out --- the likelihood is
what does the transferring.}

## Choosing a likelihood commits you

It must:

1. **express your economic model**
2. let you say which parameter values are probable
3. **let the data prove you wrong**

\vspace{0.8em}

\socratic{
Write down the likelihood for your current project.

\vspace{0.3em}
Now write down a dataset that would embarrass it.

\vspace{0.3em}
\textbf{If you can't, what have you actually assumed?}
}

## The likelihood principle

Two researchers. Same coin. Same prior.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
**A** decides to do 20 trials.

Gets 7 successes.
:::
::: {.column width="47%"}
**B** decides to stop at 7 successes.

The 7th lands on trial 20.
:::
::::

\vspace{0.6em}

Different experiments, different distributions --- **same likelihood, up to a constant.**

\vspace{0.4em}

So: **same posterior, same inference.**

## Which means the stopping rule is irrelevant

It does not matter whether you planned 20 trials, planned to stop at 7 successes, or just got
bored and quit.

\vspace{0.6em}

The frequentist answer **depends on what was in the researcher's head**.

\vspace{0.8em}

\socratic{
Would you throw away unrepeatable data because you couldn't find out what someone intended when
they started?
}

## This is what converted Savage

Savage spent the 1950s trying to rebuild statistics on Wald's foundations.

\vspace{0.5em}

The project failed --- publicly, in his own words.

\vspace{0.6em}

He said his conversion to Bayesianism came from **discovering the likelihood principle.**

\vspace{0.5em}

The idea that shocks a first-year class is the one that turned the most careful frequentist mind
of the era into *"we radical Bayesians."*

# V. Exchangeability

## The problem with "iid"

Every model starts with *"$Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ are independent and identically distributed."*

\vspace{0.6em}

But that sentence implies a **machine out there** producing draws --- probability with an
objective existence.

\vspace{0.6em}

If probability is your degree of belief, what is that sentence even saying?

## Exchangeability

\begin{block}{Definition 1.4}
Your beliefs are \textbf{exchangeable} if reordering the observations doesn't change your joint
distribution.
\end{block}

\vspace{0.6em}

- iid $\Rightarrow$ exchangeable. **Not the reverse.**
- It is a **judgement**, and it is yours.

\vspace{0.5em}

Notice the grammar: the coin isn't exchangeable. **Your beliefs are.**

## de Finetti's theorem

If your beliefs about a binary sequence are exchangeable, then

$$p(y_1,\dots,y_n) \;=\; \int \theta^{\,s}(1-\theta)^{\,n-s}\,dF(\theta)$$

\vspace{0.5em}

Look at what's on the right: **a likelihood, integrated against a prior.**

\vspace{0.7em}

\key{You never needed to assume iid. Judge your beliefs symmetric, and a likelihood \emph{and a
prior} fall out whether you wanted them or not.}

## Ask the room

\socratic{
Are daily returns on SPY exchangeable in your beliefs?

\vspace{0.4em}
If a 2008 observation and a 2017 observation were swapped, would anything change?

\vspace{0.5em}
\textbf{If yes --- you have just signed up to model the dependence.}
}

# VI. The prior

## It's yours, and you don't have to believe it

You should try other priors on purpose: *"if I had believed this, what would I now believe?"*

That's **sensitivity analysis**.

\vspace{0.6em}

You may even look at the data first. Bayes' theorem never told you what to believe --- only how
beliefs **change**.

## Two rules of thumb

\begin{block}{Encompass your audience}
A prior nobody shares makes your paper uninteresting: \emph{"So what, I don't believe A."}\\
Use one that isn't sharply inconsistent with any reasonable belief.
\end{block}

\begin{block}{Never assign zero}
Zero times anything is zero. You can never learn that the truth was there.
\end{block}

## Conjugacy is a convenience

If the prior and posterior are in the same family, you never do an integral.

Bernoulli likelihood $\times$ beta prior $\to$ beta posterior:

```julia
using Distributions
prior     = Beta(1, 1)                 # uniform: 0 prior successes, 0 failures
n, s      = 20, 7                      # 20 trials, 7 successes
posterior = Beta(1 + s, 1 + n - s)     # just add them up
mean(posterior), std(posterior)        # 0.3636, 0.1003
```

\vspace{0.3em}

**Updating is counting.** The prior is a pile of imaginary earlier trials.

\vspace{0.3em}

Conjugacy mattered when we did this by hand. Now it's a nicety.

## Where the prior stops mattering

The likelihood is essentially **zero almost everywhere**.

\vspace{0.5em}

So your prior gets multiplied by zero almost everywhere. What you believed out there is
irrelevant.

\vspace{0.7em}

\key{Least squares and maximum likelihood are flat-prior Bayes.\\
So what exactly were you objecting to?}

# VII. The posterior

## Reporting it

1. **Draw it.** For a scalar --- or a scalar function of a vector --- nothing beats the picture.
2. **Report moments.** Posterior mean and SD. Looks like your usual table.
3. **Report an HPD interval.** The shortest interval holding 95% of your belief.
4. **Report marginals.** Integrate the rest out.

\vspace{0.6em}

Only #4 is hard. Part VIII is about that.

## The sentence you are allowed to say

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
**Confidence interval**

"If I repeated this procedure many times, 95% of the intervals I'd build would cover the true
value."
:::
::: {.column width="47%"}
**HPD interval**

"The probability that $\rho$ is between 0.94 and 1.08 is 0.95."

\vspace{0.4em}
*It's as simple as that.*
:::
::::

\vspace{0.6em}

Every student who has ever misinterpreted a confidence interval was reaching for the right-hand
sentence.

## Data wins in the end

The log posterior is the log likelihood plus the log prior.

\vspace{0.5em}

Data accumulate; the likelihood term grows. **The prior term just sits there.**

\vspace{0.7em}

Three very different priors, 5 observations: still visibly different.

Same three priors, 20 observations: nearly identical.

\vspace{0.6em}

Two honest people are dragged into agreement by evidence --- **as long as neither was dogmatic,
and both agree on the likelihood.**

## Sampling the posterior

Stop trying to do the integrals. **Draw from the posterior instead.**

One row per draw, one column per parameter:

- the whole matrix is the **joint** posterior
- one column is a **marginal** --- to study $\theta_1$, *ignore the other column*
- apply any function **row-wise** and you have that function's posterior

\vspace{0.6em}

\key{If you can sample a distribution, you can know it as precisely as you like. This is the whole
modern shift --- computer power in place of hard mathematics.}

## Which lets you answer the actual question

Want the marginal effect, the elasticity, the probability an effect is positive?

\vspace{0.5em}

Compute it on **every draw**. You now have its posterior. Read off whatever you want.

\vspace{0.8em}

\socratic{
"The posterior probability that this effect is positive is 0.94."

\vspace{0.4em}
\textbf{Write down the frequentist object that answers the same question.}

\vspace{0.3em}
Take your time.
}

# VIII. When there's no conjugate prior

## Two integrals stand in the way

$$p(y) = \int p(y\mid\theta)p(\theta)\,d\theta
\qquad\qquad
p(\theta_j \mid y) = \int p(\theta\mid y)\,d\theta_{-j}$$

\vspace{0.5em}

Conjugacy made the first one disappear --- you *recognized* the answer instead of computing it.

\vspace{0.5em}

The second is the marginalization. In general: hard.

\vspace{0.6em}

**Two escapes:** approximate the posterior, or **sample** it. Sampling wins --- with an
approximation you can never check the error without doing the exact calculation you were avoiding.

## Monte Carlo is integration by sampling

Every posterior summary is an average of *something* over the posterior:

| You want | Average this over the draws |
|:--|:--|
| posterior mean | $\theta$ |
| $P(\theta > 0 \mid y)$ | 1 if $\theta>0$, else 0 |
| a marginal effect | the effect, computed per draw |
| **value at risk** | a quantile --- just sort them |

\vspace{0.5em}

**You never needed a formula for the posterior. You needed draws from it.**

## ABC: when you can simulate but not evaluate

You can run your model **forward** --- give it a $\theta$, it spits out plausible data.

You cannot write down $p(y\mid\theta)$.

\vspace{0.6em}

This is normal life for:

- structural and agent-based models
- numerically-solved equilibrium models
- anything with a simulator and no formula

## ABC is the algorithm, run forward

\begin{block}{Rejection ABC}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Draw $\theta$ from the \textbf{prior}.
\item \textbf{Simulate} a dataset from it.
\item Keep $\theta$ if the simulated data look like the real data.
\end{enumerate}
\end{block}

```julia
draws = Float64[]
for m in 1:400_000
    ts = rand(Uniform(0, 1))       # 1. from the prior
    ys = rand(Binomial(20, ts))    # 2. SIMULATE (no pdf evaluated)
    ys == 7 && push!(draws, ts)    # 3. keep it if it matches
end
mean(draws), std(draws)            # 0.3636, 0.1003  <- the exact answer
```

## Two things that just happened

\begin{block}{It was exact, not approximate}
The number of successes is \textbf{sufficient}, and we demanded an exact match. So we conditioned
on everything the data contained --- and got the conjugate answer without ever writing a
likelihood.
\end{block}

\begin{block}{The acceptance rate is $p(y)$}
$1/21 = 4.76\%$ of draws survived. That fraction \emph{is} the marginal likelihood --- the
denominator we spent all of Chapter 1 throwing away.
\end{block}

\vspace{0.3em}

And Chapter 2 uses it to check models and choose between them.

## What ABC costs you

- **Sufficient statistics are rare.** Usually you pick summaries --- so you're answering a coarser
  question than you asked.
- **Loosening the match widens the posterior.** Report your tolerance or you're reporting an
  estimate with no standard error.
- **It doesn't scale** in the number of summaries.

\vspace{0.6em}

\socratic{
ABC never evaluates a likelihood --- but you chose the summary statistic in advance.

\vspace{0.3em}
\textbf{Is that different from choosing a test statistic?}
}

# IX. Prediction

## It was there the whole time

The denominator we kept dropping:

$$p(y) = \int p(y\mid\theta)\,p(\theta)\,d\theta$$

\vspace{0.5em}

Lancaster gives it two names: the **marginal** distribution of the data, and the **predictive**
distribution of the data.

\vspace{0.7em}

\key{Writing down a likelihood and a prior \emph{is} predicting your data.\\
Model criticism is just comparing that prediction to what showed up.}

## Two predictive distributions

\begin{block}{Prior predictive}
What your data \textbf{should have looked like}, before you saw them.\\
Basis of formal model checks.
\end{block}

\begin{block}{Posterior predictive}
What \textbf{another draw} from your model should look like, now that you've seen the data.\\
A forecast, or a replication of your own dataset.
\end{block}

\vspace{0.4em}

$$p(\tilde y \mid y) = \int p(\tilde y \mid \theta)\,p(\theta\mid y)\,d\theta$$

## How to predict --- Algorithm 2.5

\begin{block}{Two steps, repeated}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Draw a $\theta$ from the posterior.
\item Draw a $\tilde y$ from the model at that $\theta$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{block}

\vspace{0.6em}

**One $\theta$ per prediction.**

\vspace{0.4em}

Your uncertainty about the parameter and the world's randomness get compounded --- not stacked
side by side, not reported separately.

## The plug-in fallacy

Standard practice: estimate $\hat\theta$, then predict as if it were correct.

\vspace{0.7em}

Lancaster: this **has no theoretical justification** except as an approximation --- and only when
the posterior is tightly concentrated.

\vspace{0.7em}

**Plug-in prediction is always too confident.** It reports the world's variability and quietly
drops yours.

\vspace{0.5em}

In the AR(1) example, the predictive precision is *always* less than the model's --- and it gets
worse when you forecast from an extreme starting point.

## Prediction is the primitive

de Finetti, one more time:

The thing you really have beliefs about is **the observables**.

$\theta$ is a device for representing those beliefs compactly.

\vspace{0.8em}

\socratic{
Which would you rather defend in a seminar --- your posterior for $\beta$, or your prediction for
next quarter?

\vspace{0.4em}
\textbf{Which one can actually be checked?}

\vspace{0.3em}
So why do our tables report the other one?
}

# X. Decisions --- and Wald

## Lancaster declines the decision frame

Many writers treat inference as **decision making**. Economists like that: their agents optimize.

\vspace{0.7em}

Lancaster says no. The econometrician's job is **reporting**:

> Draw the marginal of the object of interest, and leave it to others --- policy makers --- to
> decide.

## But loss functions are already there

Given a **loss function**, the Bayes decision minimizes **expected loss over the posterior**.

- squared error loss $\to$ report the posterior **mean**
- absolute error $\to$ the **median**
- 0--1 loss $\to$ the **mode**

\vspace{0.7em}

\key{The "estimate" you report is a statement about your loss function --- not about your beliefs.}

## An example with teeth

Data uniform on $0$ to $\theta$. Under squared error loss, the Bayes decision is:

**take the largest observation and nudge it up.**

\vspace{0.6em}

Maximum likelihood reports the largest observation itself --- which is **too low for essentially
every dataset that could ever occur.**

\vspace{0.7em}

The posterior didn't change between those two answers. Only the loss function did.

## Wald: statistics *is* decision theory

Marschak, 1946: von Neumann says *to be an economic man you must be a statistical man.* Wald was
arguing the reverse.

\vspace{0.6em}

**Wald's statistical decision problem:** actions, states of the world, a **loss function**, and an
experiment that costs something.

\vspace{0.5em}

A statistical answer should tell you **what to do**, not what to say. He called it *inductive
behavior*.

\vspace{0.5em}

And since Nature's choice is unknown, act as if Nature were trying to hurt you --- **minimax**,
statistics as a game.

## The twist

\begin{alertblock}{The complete class theorem (Wald, 1947)}
For any non-Bayesian decision rule there is a \textbf{Bayesian} rule at least as good.

\vspace{0.3em}
The Bayesian rules are \emph{complete}.
\end{alertblock}

\vspace{0.6em}

Wald proved it --- and then used priors "merely as mathematical tools," denying they meant
anything.

\vspace{0.5em}

**The most rigorous frequentist decision theorist of the century proved you never need to be
non-Bayesian, and declined to be a Bayesian.**

## Discussion: econometrics vs. decision theory

\small
\begin{alertblock}{For the room}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Giocoli's paradox: we model our \textbf{agents} as Bayesians and do our own estimation as
frequentists. Inconsistency, or division of labor?
\item Lancaster's answer: emphasize both perspectives \textbf{"not because econometricians take
decisions but because agents do."} Resolution or truce?
\item "Just report the marginal" --- but a report has a length, a format, and things left out.
Is that really free of a loss function?
\item If a central bank or a risk committee will act on your number, are you still only reporting?
\end{enumerate}
\end{alertblock}

# XI. Bridge to Chapter 2 --- value at risk

## Where Chapter 2 goes

- **2.1--2.2** How to check a model. QQ plots, thick tails, mixtures --- *i.e.* returns.
- **2.3** Which beliefs the data can never check.
- **2.4** Formal checks, via the **prior predictive**.
- **2.5** **Posterior prediction.**
- **2.6** Posterior odds, Bayes factors, model averaging.
- **2.7** Enlarging the model --- constant variance $\to$ **ARCH**.

\vspace{0.6em}

Chapter 2 opens: **"If you don't criticize your results you can be sure that others will."**

## VaR and ES are just facts about a distribution

- **Value at risk:** a **quantile** of the loss distribution.
- **Expected shortfall:** the **average loss beyond** that quantile.

\vspace{0.8em}

Neither is hard. The entire question is:

\vspace{0.3em}

\key{\emph{Which} distribution?\\
The model at your estimate --- or the posterior predictive?}

## Two sources of uncertainty

$$p(\tilde r \mid y) \;=\; \int
\underbrace{p(\tilde r\mid\theta)}_{\text{tomorrow's shock}}\;
\underbrace{p(\theta\mid y)}_{\text{your ignorance}}\;d\theta$$

\vspace{0.6em}

Plug-in keeps the first and drops the second.

\vspace{0.6em}

Do it properly for normal returns and the predictive distribution comes out **Student-$t$**, not
normal.

\vspace{0.4em}

\key{Some of the fat tail in your risk model isn't the market. It's you, not knowing $\theta$.}

## How much does plug-in understate the risk?

Tail multipliers, in units of $s$:

| $n$ | level | VaR plug-in | VaR predictive | ES plug-in | ES predictive |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 25 | 1% | 2.33 | **2.54** | 2.67 | **2.98** |
| 60 | 1% | 2.33 | **2.41** | 2.67 | **2.79** |
| 250 | 1% | 2.33 | **2.35** | 2.67 | **2.69** |

\vspace{0.4em}

Biggest correction exactly where risk management is hardest: **short samples, deep tails.**

\vspace{0.3em}

And ES is corrected more than VaR.

## Predictive VaR in three lines

```julia
# draw parameters from the posterior, then returns from the model
sigma2 = nu * s2 ./ rand(Chisq(nu), M)            # step 1
mu     = rbar .+ sqrt.(sigma2 ./ n) .* randn(M)
rtilde = mu .+ sqrt.(sigma2) .* randn(M)          # step 2

q   = quantile(rtilde, 0.01)
VaR = -q
ES  = -mean(rtilde[rtilde .<= q])
```

\vspace{0.3em}

Same two steps as Algorithm 2.5 --- **and this works when the model is a GARCH, a jump diffusion,
or a simulator you can only run forward.**

## VaR itself has a posterior

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
**Predictive VaR** --- one number.

Your uncertainty is already averaged in. This is what you hold capital against.
:::
::: {.column width="47%"}
**Posterior of VaR** --- a whole distribution.

VaR is a function of $\theta$, so compute it on every draw.
:::
::::

\vspace{0.6em}

60 days of returns, 1% level: point estimate **0.0247**, but the posterior says

$$[\,0.0205,\; 0.0304\,]$$

**Your VaR is known to about $\pm 20\%$.** The report shows three decimals and no interval.

## Ask the room

\socratic{
\begin{enumerate}
\item Which number does a capital requirement need --- and which does a risk \emph{committee} need?
\item Backtesting counts exceedances over many days. That is a repeated-sampling check on a
Bayesian number. Incoherent, or exactly right?
\item Expected shortfall is an \textbf{expected loss}. That is Wald's risk function wearing a Basel
hat. \textbf{Did the regulators become Bayesians, or Waldians?}
\end{enumerate}
}

## One last thread

Are returns exchangeable? **No** --- 2008 and 2017 are not swappable.

\vspace{0.6em}

So you model the dependence: that's ARCH, GARCH, stochastic volatility. Chapter 2's "enlarging the
model."

\vspace{0.6em}

Then place your exchangeability judgement one level down --- on the **standardized** returns.

\vspace{0.5em}

**That judgement is checkable. And it is where the tail risk lives.**

# Close

## The chapter in one slide

\begin{block}{ALGORITHM 1.1}
\textbf{1.} likelihood \quad \textbf{2.} prior \quad \textbf{3.} data \quad
\textbf{4.} Bayes' theorem \quad \textbf{5.} criticize
\end{block}

- **Likelihood** --- the only door the data come through.
- **Exchangeability** --- judge your beliefs symmetric, and you already have a prior.
- **Prior** --- yours, revisable, never dogmatic.
- **Posterior** --- don't integrate it. **Sample it.**
- **Prediction** --- the observables are what you can actually check.
- **$p(y)$**, the thing we kept dropping, is the predictive distribution --- and it's where
  Chapter 2, model choice, and every risk number live.

## Take these with you

1. Rewrite one table from a paper you admire as a Bayesian would report it.
2. Write down a dataset that would embarrass your own model.
3. Simulate the two stopping rules. Confirm the posteriors agree and the p-values don't.
4. Decide the level at which you'd call your data exchangeable, and defend it.
5. Compute plug-in VaR, predictive VaR, and the posterior of VaR --- then argue for the number
   you'd hand a risk committee.

\vspace{0.5em}

**Sources:** Lancaster (2004) Ch. 1, Ch. 2, Appendix 1 $\cdot$ Giocoli (2013), *From Wald to Savage*
$\cdot$ full detail in the extended deck.
